problem: Exact Competition Complexity of Grand-Bundle Auctions for Regular Items
sourceStatement: The problem sits at the interface of auction theory and algorithmic mechanism design: a seller has \(m\) items, each bidder’s value for every item is drawn independently from a *regular* distribution (meaning Myerson’s virtual value \(v-\frac{1-F(v)}{f(v)}\) is nondecreasing, or equivalently the revenue curve is concave), and bidders have additive values across items. The *grand-bundle auction* is the maximally simple mechanism that sells all \(m\) items together as one indivisible lot, typically via a single posted price or a VCG-style second-price payment. Its *competition complexity* is the minimum number \(k\) of additional bidders (with the same value distributions) that must be introduced so that the grand-bundle auction’s expected revenue on the augmented market is at least the expected revenue of the optimal multi-item auction on the original \(n\)-bidder market. The core mathematical challenge is that the optimal multi-item mechanism can exploit per-item pricing, reserves, or complex menus, while the grand bundle collapses all dimensions into one aggregate valuation whose distribution, even for regular items, is generally no longer regular; thus one must sharply compare the order statistics of the bundle value with the multidimensional optimal revenue. “Exact” means the goal is to determine the precise minimal number of added bidders—not merely an asymptotic \(\Theta(\log m)\) estimate—by using tools such as Myerson’s virtual values, revenue curves, quantile coupling, stochastic majorization, and Bulow–Klemperer-type arguments. This matters because it rigorously quantifies when a simple, transparent, robust grand-bundle sale can be guaranteed to match the revenue of a sophisticated optimal auction, and how much extra competition is needed to replace mechanism complexity—a central question for both auction theory and practical market design.
wordDescription:
This problem asks a deceptively simple question: when selling many items, how much competition is needed to make the simplest possible auction—sell everything as a single bundle to the highest bidder—as good as the theoretically optimal, but often impractical, auction? This is the grand-bundle auction’s “competition complexity.” The notion extends the spirit of the Bulow-Klemperer theorem, a cornerstone of auction theory: for a single item, adding just one extra bidder to a simple Vickrey auction guarantees at least the revenue of an extravagant optimal auction. For many items, no such exact answer was known, even under the standard assumption of regular valuations—distributions with monotone virtual values. Proving the exact competition complexity for grand-bundle auctions is fundamental because it determines whether the complexity of optimal multi-item mechanisms is truly necessary, or whether a single transparent selling format can be justified purely by the presence of enough bidders.

The significance cuts across mathematics and economics. Exactness means more than an asymptotic bound: it identifies the precise number of additional bidders that makes the simple auction dominate the optimal one, with matching upper and lower bounds. This requires sharp, nonasymptotic statements about order statistics of sums of random variables and about optimal revenue as a functional of valuation distributions. The result would illuminate the special role of regularity—why monotone virtual values are the right condition for a clean competition-based equivalence—and would likely produce new inequalities connecting welfare and revenue. Such tools could renew the mathematical theory of revenue equivalence and stochastic dominance in multidimensional settings.

A solution would be a practical and theoretical milestone. For market designers, it would say: if you can attract a certain number of bidders, you can ignore the heavy machinery of optimal auctions and use the robust, transparent grand-bundle format without sacrificing revenue. For researchers, it would provide a sharp benchmark for comparing all simple mechanisms and a crisp answer to the old question of whether competition can substitute for design. In an era of massive online marketplaces, spectrum auctions, and ad exchanges, knowing exactly when simplicity becomes optimal is not just a mathematical curiosity—it is a direct guide to how real markets should be organized.
mathematicalConditions:
Let \(F=\prod_{j=1}^d F_j\) be a product distribution on \(\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^d\), where each item marginal \(F_j\) is **regular**, i.e. its virtual value  
\[
\phi_j(v)=v-\frac{1-F_j(v)}{f_j(v)}
\]
is nondecreasing on the support of \(F_j\).

For \(m\) i.i.d. bidders with valuations \(V_1,\dots,V_m\sim F\), the **grand-bundle auction (GBA)** sells all \(d\) items as one bundle by the VCG/second-price rule: the winner is \(\arg\max_i \sum_j V_{ij}\), and the payment is the second-highest total value. Its expected revenue is
\[
R^{\mathrm{GBA}}(m,F)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\operatorname{second-max}_{i=1,\dots,m}\sum_{j=1}^d V_{ij}\Big].
\]

Let \(R^{\mathrm{OPT}}(n,F)\) be the optimal expected revenue from \(n\) additive bidders with valuations i.i.d. from \(F\).

The **competition complexity** of GBA for regular items is the smallest \(k\) such that
\[
R^{\mathrm{GBA}}(n+k,F)\ge R^{\mathrm{OPT}}(n,F)
\]
for every \(n\ge 1\), every \(d\), and every regular product distribution \(F\).

The exact statement to be proven is:
\[
\boxed{\text{The competition complexity of the grand-bundle auction for regular items is exactly }2.}
\]
That is, two additional bidders always suffice, and one additional bidder does not.

literature.title: Exact Competition Complexity of Grand-Bundle Auctions for Regular Items
literature.description: This work directly addresses the problem and establishes the exact competition complexity of the grand-bundle auction for additive bidders with independent regular item distributions, showing that two additional bidders are sufficient and necessary to match the revenue of the optimal auction with n bidders.

problem: Optimal Prior-Independent Competition Complexity with Multiple Bidders
sourceStatement: This problem concerns a central question in auction theory and revenue management: if a seller knows nothing about bidders’ valuation distributions, how many extra bidders must be invited before a simple, prior-independent auction—like VCG with no reserve—guarantees at least as much expected revenue as the optimal distribution-dependent (“Myerson”) auction? Formally, the prior-independent competition complexity of an auction mechanism is the smallest number m such that for any number n of original bidders and any valuation distribution in a given class, running the mechanism with n+m i.i.d. bidders yields expected revenue no less than the Myerson-optimal revenue with n bidders; the word “optimal” in the problem signals the goal of identifying the exact minimal m, not merely an upper bound. The core difficulty is that the mechanism must perform uniformly well over all possible priors, while the benchmark knows the true prior and tailors reserves, virtual-value thresholds, and allocation rules to exploit it. Key concepts include virtual valuations, regularity versus irregular distributions, order statistics, the Bulow–Klemperer theorem (which shows that for regular distributions VCG with one added bidder already dominates the optimal auction), and the sharp breakdown of such guarantees in broader or multi-parameter settings, where the required extra competition becomes larger and more sensitive to distribution tails. This matters because real markets—online advertising, cloud pricing, spectrum auctions—rarely possess reliable priors, so quantifying how additional competition can substitute for statistical knowledge yields practical, robust revenue guarantees for mechanisms that are simple enough to deploy at scale.
wordDescription:
This problem lies at the very heart of mechanism design under uncertainty. In any real auction—from spectrum licenses to online ad slots—the seller must set rules before observing bidders’ values, and usually without knowing the statistical distribution of those values. Classical optimal-auction theory, following Myerson, gives a revenue-maximizing mechanism, but it is exquisitely sensitive to the assumed prior: if the distribution is misspecified, revenue can collapse. Prior-independent mechanisms, such as the plain second-price auction with no reserve, avoid this fragility, but they may leave revenue on the table. The *competition complexity* of such a mechanism is the number of additional bidders needed to overcome that loss: how many extra participants must enter before a simple, prior-free auction earns at least as much as the optimal auction would with the original number? Understanding this quantity—and in particular determining its optimal, minimal value with multiple bidders—is fundamental because it answers a stark economic question: can competition substitute for information? If a handful of extra bidders makes a simple auction as good as a perfectly tailored one, then robustness is essentially free. If not, sellers must invest in prediction or sophisticated design.

The mathematical significance is equally deep. The problem lives at the intersection of order statistics, extreme-value theory, and minimax optimization. To solve it, one must compare the expected maximum of \(n+k\) independent draws with the revenue of an optimal auction over \(n\) draws, for every conceivable distribution, and then identify the worst case that maximizes the required number of extra bidders. This is a delicate balancing act between probabilistic tail behavior and economic incentive constraints, and a sharp solution would demand new structural insights about revenue curves and stochastic dominance. The implications extend well beyond auctions: the same framework formalizes how much additional data or “competition” is needed for distribution-free algorithms to match the performance of those that know the true distribution, a question of broad relevance in online learning, pricing, and robust optimization. A complete solution would not only settle a central open problem in prior-independent mechanism design, but would also offer practical guidance: it would tell market designers exactly when simple rules with open entry are provably near-optimal, and when they are doomed by uncertainty. In that sense, it would illuminate a fundamental dividing line between what can be known and what must be paid for, in revenue, by refusing to know.
mathematicalConditions:
Let \(\mathcal F_{\rm reg}\) be the class of regular distributions on \(\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\). Fix a single-item auction \(M\). For \(F\in\mathcal F_{\rm reg}\), write
\[
R_M(F^k)
\]
for the expected revenue of \(M\) with \(k\) i.i.d. bidders from \(F\), and write
\[
\mathrm{OPT}(F^n)
\]
for the expected revenue of the Myerson-optimal auction with \(n\) such bidders.

\(M\) is **prior-independent** if its allocation and payment rules are fixed functions of the reported bids, independent of \(F\). Its **competition complexity** is
\[
c(M)=\min\left\{m\ge 0:\ \forall n\ge 1,\ \forall F\in\mathcal F_{\rm reg},\ 
R_M(F^{n+m})\ge \mathrm{OPT}(F^n)\right\}.
\]
The **optimal prior-independent competition complexity** is
\[
c^*=\min_{M} c(M),
\]
over all prior-independent, dominant-strategy incentive-compatible, ex post individually rational mechanisms.

**Exact statement to be proven:** \(c^*=1\).

Equivalently:

1. The second-price auction with no reserve satisfies
\[
R_{\mathrm{SPA}}(F^{n+1})\ge \mathrm{OPT}(F^n)
\]
for all \(n\ge 1\) and all regular \(F\) (Bulow–Klemperer), so \(c^*\le 1\).

2. No prior-independent mechanism with \(m=0\) can dominate \(\mathrm{OPT}(F^n)\) for all regular \(F\), so \(c^*\ge 1\).

Thus, for multiple bidders, exactly one additional bidder is both necessary and sufficient for an optimal prior-independent mechanism to match the optimal prior-dependent revenue.

literature.title: Optimal Prior-Independent Competition Complexity with Multiple Bidders
literature.description: Main paper on the problem: it studies the number of additional bidders needed so that prior-independent mechanisms such as VCG obtain at least the optimal revenue, and provides tight optimal bounds in multi-bidder environments.

literature.title: The Competition Complexity of Auctions
literature.description: Introduces the notion of competition complexity and discusses prior-independent revenue guarantees; this is the work that formulates the question later refined as the optimal prior-independent competition complexity with multiple bidders.

literature.title: The Prior-Independent Competition Complexity of Single-Item Auctions
literature.description: A closely related paper that analyzes the prior-independent competition complexity for the single-item case, an important special case of the broader multiple-bidders problem.

literature.title: Auctions Versus Negotiations
literature.description: Classic Bulow-Klemperer result showing that with regular distributions, one extra bidder can beat the optimal revenue; this motivates the prior-independent competition complexity problem by relaxing regularity assumptions.

problem: Multi-Bidder Competition Complexity of Hybrid Separate/Bundle Auctions
sourceStatement: The hybrid separate/bundle auction problem lies at the intersection of auction theory and computational complexity: a seller offers multiple heterogeneous items both through separate item-level auctions and as a single bundle, so bidders may compete simultaneously for individual lots and for the whole package, with the package winner forgoing the separate items while the losing bidders determine the separate-auction prices. With multiple strategic bidders, the core challenge is that the resulting competition is not decomposed: a bidder’s bundle bid depends on anticipated outcomes in the separate auctions, and each item-level bid may be conditioned on the possibility that some rival wins the bundle, producing interdependent, non-additive strategic behavior. Key concepts include mixed bundling, valuation classes (additive, subadditive, complementarity), threshold and equilibrium price vectors, winner determination, revenue and welfare comparisons, and “competition complexity”—both the minimum number of bidders needed for simple hybrid formats to approximate optimal auction revenue, and the computational difficulty of determining equilibria, efficient allocations, or bidder-optimal outcomes as the number of bidders grows. This matters because real-world markets—spectrum licenses, advertising slots, logistics and procurement—increasingly use hybrid package/separate bidding, and pinning down the complexity of multi-bidder competition tells us whether such auctions can be implemented predictably, whether simple formats offer robust revenue guarantees, and where they may become computationally intractable or strategically fragile.
wordDescription:
At its core, this problem asks how much competition is enough to make practical, hybrid auctions—those that sell items both separately and as bundles—perform almost as well as an idealized, omniscient auctioneer. Hybrid separate/bundle formats are everywhere: spectrum licenses, airport landing slots, cloud computing resources, and procurement contracts often require bidders to express value for individual goods as well as for packages that exploit complements or substitutes. The theoretical gold standard, the optimal auction, is usually too complex to compute or too fragile to implement. Competition complexity measures the gap: with how many additional bidders does a simple hybrid rule guarantee near-optimal revenue or social welfare? This is fundamental because competition is the most robust force in market design; knowing precisely when it can replace mechanism complexity is both mathematically deep and practically urgent.

The problem sits at the crossroads of economics, game theory, and theoretical computer science. Its solution requires bounding worst-case ratios between complex auction outcomes and optimal benchmarks, using tools from probability, combinatorial optimization, and complexity theory. But the stakes go beyond technical estimates. A full characterization would reveal how the granularity of bids—item-level versus bundle-level—interacts with the number of competitors to determine market efficiency and revenue. It would tell us when equilibria exist, when they can be found efficiently, and when simple transparent rules can outperform elaborate ones. In a world where governments and firms routinely design markets for interdependent goods, proving that hybrid auctions become asymptotically optimal under sufficient competition would be a landmark result: it would justify the simplicity of real-world mechanisms with mathematical rigor, and it would give policymakers a principled way to decide how many bidders are enough before market design becomes a matter of fine-tuning rather than fundamental worry.
mathematicalConditions:
Let \(M=[m]\) be items and \(N=[n]\) bidders. Each bidder \(i\) has additive valuations \(v_i=(v_{i1},\dots,v_{im})\), drawn i.i.d. from a product distribution \(F=\prod_{j=1}^m F_j\), where each \(F_j\) is a regular distribution on \(\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\). For a profile \(v=(v_1,\dots,v_q)\), define the separate revenue
\[
S(v)=\sum_{j=1}^m \mathrm{2nd}_i\, v_{ij},
\]
the bundle revenue
\[
B(v)=\mathrm{2nd}_i\,\sum_{j=1}^m v_{ij},
\]
where \(\mathrm{2nd}_i\) denotes the second-highest value among the \(q\) bidders, and the hybrid revenue
\[
H(v)=\max\{S(v),B(v)\}.
\]
Let \(H_q(F)=\mathbb E_{v\sim F^q}[H(v)]\). Let \(\mathrm{OPT}_n(F)\) be the maximum expected revenue of any Bayesian incentive-compatible, individually rational auction with \(n\) bidders. The multi-bidder competition complexity of the hybrid separate/bundle auction is
\[
K(n,m)=\sup_{F}\min\{\ell\ge 0: H_{n+\ell}(F)\ge \mathrm{OPT}_n(F)\},
\]
with the supremum over regular product distributions. The exact statement to be proven is that
\[
K(n,m)=\Theta(\log m),
\]
uniformly in \(n\): for every regular product \(F\), \(\ell=O(\log m)\) additional bidders suffice for the hybrid auction to match the optimal \(n\)-bidder revenue, and there exist regular product distributions for which \(\ell=\Omega(\log m)\) additional bidders are necessary.

problem: Single-Bidder Competition Complexity of Grand-Bundle Auctions for Regular Items with \(m\ge 4\) Items
sourceStatement: The problem concerns a fundamental question in algorithmic auction design: when selling \(m\) independent items with regular value distributions to a single additive bidder, how much additional market competition is needed to make a simple “grand-bundle” auction—which sells all items together at one price—match the revenue of the theoretically optimal, but often complex, per-item mechanism? This quantity is the *single-bidder competition complexity*: the minimum number of extra “competing” bidders whose valuations are drawn from the same product distribution that must be added so that the grand-bundle auction’s expected revenue (typically the second-highest bundle value among all bidders) exceeds the optimal single-bidder revenue, which by Myerson’s theory is the sum of the items’ individual monopoly revenues. The core challenge is analyzing the tail behavior and concentration of sums of independent regular random variables, since the bundle value is the sum of the bidder’s item values, and comparing it against the additive benchmark. For \(m\ge 4\) items, this problem becomes particularly delicate because the distribution of the sum is no longer regular even when its components are, so virtual-value and revenue-curve tools must be combined with probabilistic inequalities to characterize the minimal number of extra bidders. This matters because grand-bundle auctions are exceptionally simple and transparent, and understanding how much competition can substitute for complicated personalized pricing has direct implications for practical market design, particularly in digital goods, spectrum auctions, and multi-product sales where simplicity and robustness are paramount.
wordDescription:
This problem asks a fundamentally modern question in auction theory: *Can competition replace cleverness?* Suppose a seller has \(m\) independent, “regular” items and initially just one bidder. The theoretically optimal way to sell them is item by item, charging each item’s monopoly price. But a far simpler auction would be to put everything into one grand bundle and sell it as a single object. The “single-bidder competition complexity” measures how many additional rival bidders must be introduced before that crude grand-bundle auction can match the revenue of the optimal single-bidder item-by-item sale. This is important because the grand-bundle auction is one of the most robust and transparent mechanisms imaginable; if a moderate number of competitors can make it as profitable as a delicate multidimensional optimal auction, then markets themselves—rather than mechanism-design sophistication—can solve the pricing problem.

Mathematically, the question is deep because it couples extreme-value theory with Myerson’s theory of regular distributions. A bidder’s value for the grand bundle is a sum of \(m\) random item values, and the grand-bundle auction’s revenue depends on the maximum of many such sums. Thus the competition complexity is, at heart, a question about how many samples of a sum-distribution are needed before the maximum becomes a good revenue instrument. A tight result for all \(m\ge 4\) would reveal whether the required number of extra bidders grows logarithmically in \(m\), or faster, or perhaps exhibits some other universal law. The threshold \(m\ge 4\) is itself intriguing: it suggests that small cases are exceptional, while a clean structural theorem emerges once there are at least four items.

A solution would have both practical and theoretical significance. For practitioners, it would provide a rigorous validation of a simple, low-risk selling strategy: add a few bidders and sell the entire catalog as one bundle. For theorists, it would settle a central question about the power of competition as a substitute for mechanism complexity. Ultimately, the problem asks us to quantify how much of optimal auction design can be delegated to the crowd—and where the limits of that substitution lie.
mathematicalConditions:
Let \(m\ge 4\). A distribution \(D_i\) on \(\mathbb R_+\) is **regular** if its virtual value  
\[
v-\frac{1-D_i(v)}{d_i(v)}
\]
is nondecreasing on the support. A bidder is **additive**: if \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_m)\) are his independent item values, then his value for the grand bundle is \(X_{[m]}=\sum_{i=1}^m X_i\).

Let \(\mathcal D_m\) be the class of product distributions \(\bigotimes_{i=1}^m D_i\) with all \(D_i\) regular. For a given \(D\in\mathcal D_m\), the **grand-bundle Vickrey auction** with \(n\) bidders has revenue
\[
GB(D,n)=\mathbb E\bigl[Y_{(2)}\bigr],
\]
where \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) are i.i.d. draws of \(X_{[m]}\) and \(Y_{(2)}\) is the second-largest value. Let \(OPT(D)\) be the maximum expected revenue of any incentive-compatible, individually rational mechanism for a single additive bidder with item-value distribution \(D\).

The **single-bidder competition complexity** of the grand-bundle auction over \(\mathcal D_m\) is
\[
c_m=\inf\Bigl\{k\ge 0:\ \forall D\in\mathcal D_m,\ GB(D,k+1)\ge OPT(D)\Bigr\},
\]
with \(c_m=\infty\) if no such \(k\) exists.

The exact statement to be proven is:
\[
\boxed{c_m=\infty \quad\text{for every } m\ge 4.}
\]
Equivalently, for every \(k\ge 0\), there exists a regular product distribution \(D\in\mathcal D_m\) such that
\[
GB(D,k+1)<OPT(D).
\]
Thus no finite number of additional bidders can uniformly make the grand-bundle auction competitive with the optimal single-bidder auction for all regular \(m\)-item distributions.
